item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports history perturbation as a test of model dependence. [Scarcelli et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) search for minimal sequence edits that change recommendations using genetic algorithms, reporting near-one model fidelity across three datasets and three models. A [2026 temporal-attribution study](https://jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525) evaluates deletion faithfulness, robustness, k-sufficiency and mask-versus-shuffle consistency; its results show architecture-dependent attribution, with GRU4Rec emphasizing recent interactions and transformers distributing attribution more broadly. These findings concern model behavior, not identification of users’ causal preferences.\n\nShuffling needs careful interpretation. [Liu et al. (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that arbitrary history shuffling mixes behavioral sequence effects with item-availability effects; constrained shuffling preserves availability. [Spotify’s October 2026 analysis](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) distinguishes last-item, additive pairwise and contextualized transformer models, highlighting recency weighting and training objectives as competing explanations for performance. A practical diagnostic synthesis: pair recent-history deletion and removal of repeated interests with equal-size random-removal controls; shuffle earlier interactions while preserving the last item; measure original recommendation score drops, rank changes and top-10 overlap using fixed candidates. Separate repeated item IDs from recurring title/description themes. Control padding and positional shifts, and report paired uncertainty by category. Sensitivity exceeding controls suggests dependence on selected evidence; weak sensitivity alone cannot distinguish redundant history, weak order signal or encoder failure. Keep these diagnostics separate from macro validation HR@10."}
